card: Three C1 uses of the imperfective. **The fact of an action**: *has it ever happened?* **Ты чита́л «Войну́ и мир»?** **An undone result**: it happened, but the result is gone: **Ко мне приходи́л брат** (he came and left). **Invitation**: **Сади́тесь! Проходи́те!** sounds warmer than the perfective.

sections.body: Beyond process and result, the imperfective names the fact of an action without focusing on its result. This is where even advanced learners pick the perfective and sound slightly off.

sections.title: The fact of an action
sections.body: Asking or saying *whether* something happened takes the imperfective, even for one finished action: **Вы смотре́ли э́тот фильм?** — **Да, смотре́л.** **Кто писа́л э́то письмо́?** asks who the author is. The perfective asks about a specific expected result: **Ты посмотре́л фильм, кото́рый я тебе́ дал?**

sections.title: An undone result
sections.body: With motion verbs and a few others, the imperfective past means *went and came back*, *did and undid*: **Я брал твою́ кни́гу** (it's back now). **Кто открыва́л окно́?** (it's shut now, but someone opened it). Compare **Кто откры́л окно́?**: it's open now.

sections.title: Imperatives
sections.body: Perfective imperatives are neutral requests: **Сядь, пожа́луйста.** Imperfective ones invite (**Сади́тесь!**, **Проходи́те!**), urge (**Ну, говори́ же!**) or, with **не**, forbid. With **не**, the perfective is a warning: **Не упади́!** (*Mind you don't fall!*)

mistakes.why: *Have you ever…?* asks about the fact: the imperfective.
A warning against an accident takes **не** + perfective.

examples.en: My brother came to see me yesterday (and left).
Who opened the window? (it's shut again)
